n: In this lesson we study functional poisons. The plan has six parts. First, the general characterisation and subgroups of functional poisons are considered. Then cyanides: sources, doses and mechanism of action, then the clinical picture of cyanides, post-mortem signs and diagnosis. The fourth part is hydrogen sulphide: properties, degrees of poisoning and changes in the body. Then organophosphorus compounds, that is, OPCs: cholinesterase and clinical picture. Finally post-mortem signs in OPC poisoning, diagnosis and teaching cases.

Introduction to section 6.9: functional poisons, in brief. Functional poisons act mainly on the central nervous system. They usually do not cause marked morphological changes. Therefore diagnosis rests on the circumstances, the clinical picture and laboratory results. Functional poisons are divided into four subgroups. That is, in such poisonings few conspicuous changes are found in the body, so the circumstances of the incident and laboratory examination take the main place.

The subgroups of functional poisons are given in Table 6.1; there are four. The first is those paralysing the central nervous system: cyanides, organophosphorus compounds and hydrogen sulphide. The second is those depressing the central nervous system: alcohols, hypnotics and tranquillisers. The third is stimulants: convulsant poisons, antidepressants, caffeine, amphetamines, cocaine and opiates. The fourth subgroup acts mainly on the peripheral nervous system: cholinergic and adrenergic substances and anticholinesterase substances, for example proserin and OPCs.

t: Poisons paralysing the CNS: three substances
n: In the subgroup paralysing the central nervous system, three substances are important. The first is hydrocyanic acid and its salts; their point of action is the iron of cytochrome oxidase. The second is hydrogen sulphide; its point of action is also the iron of cytochrome oxidase. The third is organophosphorus compounds; their point of action is the enzyme cholinesterase. Thus the first two substances act on the same point, whereas organophosphorus compounds act on a different enzyme.

The second section: cyanides, in brief. Cyanides block the enzyme of tissue respiration. This group includes hydrocyanic acid and potassium cyanide. More often the source is kernels of apricot, peach and plum stones. The lethal dose: for HCN 0.05 g, for KCN 0.1–0.2 g. As an antidote, methaemoglobin-forming substances are used. The body has a bitter almond odour. Remember these five points in the order of the table.

Hydrocyanic acid and potassium cyanide. Hydrocyanic acid, that is, HCN, is a colourless, volatile liquid with a bitter almond odour. In pure form it is found only in the laboratory. Potassium cyanide is a white substance, readily soluble in water. In forensic practice potassium cyanide is more important; its forensic significance is greater. Poisoning with pure cyanide is rare. That is, in practice the substance in salt form is more often important.

Sources of cyanide. Poisoning occurs more often through eating stone kernels. In addition, cyanide is released in steel and coke production and in fires. The stone kernel contains the glycoside amygdalin. Gastrointestinal enzymes break it down. As a result hydrocyanic acid is formed. Remember this chain in order: glycoside, enzyme action, then appearance of the poison.

Cyanide: lethal doses and medium. The general toxic action depends on the acidity of the medium. The lethal dose for hydrocyanic acid is 0.05 g, for potassium cyanide 0.1–0.2 g. In an acid medium the action is intensified. In an alkaline medium, by contrast, the action is weakened. This means that the acid medium of the stomach contributes to intensifying the poison, while an alkaline medium weakens it.

The mechanism of action of cyanide. The cyanide anion binds the iron of cytochrome oxidase. The poison is not metabolised and is eliminated in urine and breath. The process runs like this: CN⁻ attaches to the iron of the enzyme. The enzyme's activity is disrupted. There is oxygen in the blood, but tissue hypoxia develops. Finally, vital centres are paralysed. Remember: even if there is enough oxygen in the blood, the tissue cannot use it.

The clinical picture of cyanide depends on the amount of poison. In a large dose, in the first minute consciousness is lost, the pupils dilate, convulsions appear and death occurs. In a smaller dose, signs begin after several minutes: headache, dizziness, vomiting, tachycardia, dyspnoea and convulsions. Such a state lasts up to 40 minutes, sometimes hours. Thus the larger the dose, the faster and more severe the clinical picture.

Poisoning from stone kernels. With stone kernels there is a latent period. The latent period lasts several hours. Signs intensify more slowly. Death occurs within the first days. The source is kernels of stones of fleshy fruit. That is, unlike pure cyanide, here the poison is released gradually, which is why signs begin later.

t: Cyanide: the principle of the antidote
n: The principle of the antidote for cyanide. Methaemoglobin-forming substances can be used as an antidote. The mechanism is this: the methaemoglobin-forming substance detaches the cyanide anion from the cytochromes. After that tissue respiration is restored. This means that the poison itself becomes bound not to the enzyme but to methaemoglobin, and the enzyme begins to work again.

Cyanide: external signs in the body. There are additional signs besides the signs of rapid death. Cadaveric lividity is cherry-reddish. A bitter almond odour may be noticed from the cavities, lungs and brain. On persistence of the odour: because it is volatile, it may disappear quickly. With nitrobenzene, by contrast, the odour persists longer. Therefore it is important to detect the odour at once, otherwise it may disappear.

t: Cyanide: findings in blood and stomach
n: Cyanide: findings in blood and stomach. Findings depend on the type of substance. The blood is fluid and dark red, but bright in a large dose. With potassium cyanide, potassium hydroxide forms as a result of hydrolysis. The gastric mucosa is swollen and reddish. With stone kernels a white powder and fragments of brown shell are found. Forensic chemical examination is of great importance in diagnosis.

The third section: hydrogen sulphide, in brief. Hydrogen sulphide is a gas with a smell of rotten eggs. It accumulates in mines, sewers and cesspits. The usual cause is an accident. By mechanism it binds the iron of cytochrome oxidase. The fulminant form is seen at a concentration in the air of 1 % or more. In the body the smell of rotten eggs and cherry-red blood are found.

Properties and accumulation of hydrogen sulphide. It is a colourless gas with a smell of rotten eggs. Its molecular weight is greater than that of air, so the gas accumulates, being heavier than air. Formation: in putrefaction of sulphur-containing organic substances, and also in decomposition of rocks and minerals. Places of accumulation: mines, the sewer system and pits for storing effluent. That is, the gas collects in low, closed places and creates danger.

Entry and elimination of hydrogen sulphide. A small part is eliminated through the lungs unchanged. The permissible amount is 10 mg/m³. The main route of entry is the respiratory tract, with additional entry through skin and mucous membranes. Elimination is mainly in oxidised form. Thus the gas enters mainly by breathing and is eliminated from the body in changed form.

Types of action of hydrogen sulphide. Its toxicity is high, and it acts like cyanides. In general toxic action it binds the iron of cytochrome and cytochrome oxidase, tissue respiration enzymes are disrupted, and it acts mainly on the nervous system. In local action it irritates the mucosa of the respiratory tract and also the ocular mucosa. Thus this gas causes both general and local harm.

Degrees of poisoning with hydrogen sulphide. The clinical picture varies from mild to the fulminant form. In the mild degree the airways and ocular mucosa are irritated. In the moderate degree encephalopathy, bronchitis, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema and cardiac disturbance are observed. In the severe degree there are convulsions and coma. The fulminant form, that is, at a concentration of 1 % or more, runs with paralysis of the respiratory centre and rapid death.

t: Hydrogen sulphide: the body and diagnosis
n: Hydrogen sulphide: the body and diagnosis. The composition of the air at the scene is of particular importance. The body shows signs of rapid death. A smell of rotten eggs comes from the cavities and organs. Blood and internal organs are cherry-red in tint. The basis of diagnosis: circumstances, clinical picture, the body and toxicology. That is, the conclusion rests not on one sign but on the joint assessment of these four sources.

We compare cyanide and hydrogen sulphide. The mechanism is similar; the odour and source differ. Of the cyanides, HCN is a liquid and KCN a white substance, whereas hydrogen sulphide is a colourless gas. Odour: bitter almond with cyanides, rotten eggs with hydrogen sulphide. In both the mechanism is the same, that is, the iron of cytochrome oxidase. In the body with cyanides the lividity is cherry-reddish, with hydrogen sulphide the blood is cherry-red. The usual cause with cyanides is stone kernels and fire, with hydrogen sulphide an accident.

The fourth section: OPCs, in brief. OPCs suppress cholinesterase activity. They are used as insecticides, herbicides and fungicides. Routes of entry are respiratory, oral and healthy skin. By mechanism, acetylcholine accumulates. In the body, miosis, abundant mucus and rigor mortis are observed. In late death, however, OPCs may not be found. Remember these points.

Use of OPCs and circumstances of poisoning. The poison enters through the respiratory tract, mouth and skin. Use: in the household as an insecticide, in agriculture as a herbicide, defoliant and fungicide. Among circumstances of poisoning, most are accidents, and suicide is sometimes encountered. Toxicomaniacs also use them. That is, because these substances are widespread, the likelihood of poisoning is high.

OPC substances and lethal doses. Chlorophos, carbophos and thiophos are more often met with. The lethal dose of chlorophos is 630–660 mg/kg, and the lethal dose of thiophos 4–13 mg. The most frequently encountered substances are chlorophos and carbophos. Feature of entry: they are fat-soluble. These figures show that the degree of toxicity of the substances differs.

The mechanism of action of OPCs. OPCs are also called anticholinesterase substances. The local action is weak or absent altogether. The mechanism is this: first cholinesterase activity is suppressed. Then acetylcholine accumulates in the tissue. As a result the cholinergic system is excited. Remember: the signs of poisoning arise precisely from the excess of acetylcholine.

t: OPCs: first signs depend on route of entry
n: OPCs: first signs depend on the route of entry. On contact with the skin, local fibrillation of muscles is observed. When taken by mouth, gastroenteritis begins: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. By the inhalation route, dyspnoea and miosis appear. Thus from the first signs one can suppose by which route the poison entered.

The developed clinical picture of OPC poisoning. Disturbance of breathing, heart and vision is added. In the respiratory system there is bronchospasm and much mucus is secreted. In the cardiovascular system there is bradycardia and pressure falls. In the eye, miosis and spasm of accommodation are observed. Vision is disturbed, and in some cases lost. Thus several systems are affected at the same time.

OPCs: late stages and death. Death usually occurs on the first day. Later paraesthesia, disturbance of speech and gait, and tremor appear. In the last stage clonic-tonic convulsions are observed. Then coma begins. Death occurs from paralysis of the respiratory centre or respiratory muscles. That is, the process goes from nervous signs to convulsions and coma, and from them to respiratory paralysis.

t: OPCs: the body, early and late death
n: OPCs: the signs in the body differ in early and late death. Signs in the body depend on the time of death. In early death rigor mortis is rapid and strong, the pupils are constricted, and there is much mucus in the airways. In the intestine, spastically contracted areas are found, and in the internal organs small haemorrhages. In late death no characteristic changes are found. In the parenchymatous organs degeneration, haemorrhages under the pleura, epicardium and endocardium, cerebral oedema and bilateral focal pneumonia are observed.

t: OPCs: the body according to route of entry
n: OPCs: findings in the body vary according to the route of entry. The route by which the poison entered influences the findings in the body. When taken by mouth, catarrhal gastroenteritis is found. By the inhalation route, catarrhal tracheobronchitis and pulmonary oedema occur. With both routes small haemorrhages are seen in the internal organs. Thus the finding helps to determine the route of entry of the poison.

Laboratory diagnosis of OPCs. The method of examination depends on the time of death. In early death, forensic chemical examination of internal organs is carried out, and cholinesterase activity is also determined in blood, brain and myocardium. In late death OPCs may not be found. In such a case cholinesterase activity is below normal. That is, even if the poison itself is not found, reduced enzyme activity indicates poisoning.

Teaching case one: stone kernels. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: a child ate many apricot stone kernels. For several hours nothing was noticed. Then dyspnoea and convulsions began. In the body cherry-reddish lividity and an almond odour were found. Questions: which poison? Why did signs begin late? What may be found in the intestine? First answer yourself.

The answer to the first case: cyanide. The set of signs corresponds to cyanides. The most suitable poison is cyanides, derived from amygdalin. The reason signs began late is a latent period of several hours. Mechanism: the iron of cytochrome oxidase is bound. In the intestine a white powder and fragments of brown shell may be found. Confirmation is obtained by forensic chemical examination.

Teaching case two: field work. This too is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: a person who fell ill during chemical treatment in the field. There is dyspnoea, and the pupils are narrow. Much mucus was secreted in the airways. Bradycardia, then convulsions and coma were observed. Questions: which group of poisons? What is the mechanism of action? Which enzyme is examined? Think about the answer.

The answer to the second case: organophosphorus compounds. The signs correspond to OPC poisoning. The most suitable group is organophosphorus compounds. The mechanism is suppression of cholinesterase. Signs: miosis, bronchospasm and bradycardia. In early death forensic chemical examination and cholinesterase activity are examined. In late death, however, OPCs may not be found.

Conclusion: three paralysing poisons. In functional poisons there are few morphological changes, and diagnosis rests on circumstances, clinical picture and laboratory. The mechanism of cyanide is linked with the iron of cytochrome oxidase; in the body there are cherry-reddish lividity and an almond odour. The mechanism of hydrogen sulphide is also the iron of cytochrome oxidase; in the body a smell of rotten eggs and cherry-red blood are found. The mechanism of OPCs is suppression of cholinesterase; in the body miosis, abundant mucus and rapid rigidity are observed.

The review questions rest on the review questions of the textbook. Why are morphological signs few in functional poisons? On what is diagnosis based in cyanides? What are the mechanism of cyanide and the principle of the antidote? What degrees are distinguished in hydrogen sulphide? What are the mechanism of OPCs and the signs in the body? By answering these questions, consolidate the lesson.
